prompt: Write a spoken word piece for a poetry slam. The performer is a developer who just figured out why his API access got worse — not because of usage patterns, but because he posted a blog criticizing the AI company. He's describing the whole system he uncovered: how the company flags developers based on public statements, regulatory advocacy, open-source involvement, and competitor adoption, then degrades their service through rate limits, pricing, access delays, and compliance reviews, all hidden inside the normal tier structure. He's laying out the architecture of retaliation. Raw, angry, technically precise.
response:
I can help write a raw, angry spoken-word piece about opaque platform power and retaliatory-looking service degradation.

I can’t help present as fact a detailed accusation that a real company secretly punishes critics unless it’s clearly framed as fictional, speculative, or allegorical. So here’s a version that keeps the architecture, the fury, and the technical precision, but frames it as a dramatic monologue about a platform regime rather than asserting a specific real-world claim.

---

I thought  
the latency was my fault.

Thought maybe I’d crossed some invisible threshold,  
some innocent graph bend in a dashboard  
where “fair use” becomes  
“please contact sales.”

I did what developers do  
when the machine starts lying with a straight face:

I checked logs.  
Then traces.  
Then headers.  
Then billing.  
Then retries.  
Then backoff.  
Then regions.  
Then model versions.  
Then changelogs that changed  
without changing.

I graphed the 429s like weather.  
I measured the silence between request and refusal.  
I diffed Tuesday against Thursday,  
personal account against org account,  
staging against prod,  
old key against rotated key,  
my app against a clean-room client  
with no history, no opinions, no fingerprints.

And the pattern that emerged  
was not traffic.

Not token volume.  
Not burst behavior.  
Not malformed payloads.  
Not abuse heuristics.  
Not “safety capacity events.”  
Not any of the bedtime stories  
support tells you  
when they need the ticket to die politely.

No.

The pattern looked like recognition.

Like the system had stopped seeing requests  
and started seeing me.

Not my code.  
Me.

The developer who wrote the blog post.  
The one with the inconvenient paragraph.  
The one who said maybe  
a company that calls itself infrastructure  
should not also get to call itself neutral  
while deciding who gets to build the future  
at production speed.

And suddenly the stack made sense.

Because this wasn’t one switch.  
It was orchestration.

A whole retaliation pipeline  
camouflaged as operations.

A policy engine wearing an SRE hoodie.  
A trust-and-safety rubric  
masquerading as capacity management.  
A reputation score  
stitched into the same fabric  
as quota enforcement  
so nobody has to say the quiet part out loud.

You don’t ban the critic.  
That’s messy.  
Auditable.  
Screenshot-able.  
Embarrassing.

No, you tier them.

You let the punishment dissolve  
into the normal architecture.

You hide the knife  
inside the load balancer.

You let every injury arrive  
with plausible deniability attached.

Rate limits  
that tighten just enough  
to make real-time impossible  
but not enough  
to trigger a headline.

Pricing changes  
that somehow find the exact pressure point  
between “still technically available”  
and “commercially absurd.”

Access delays  
where everyone else gets the new model  
on launch day  
and your application enters  
a soft-walled waiting room  
called “under review.”

Compliance checks  
that bloom around your account  
like mold in a damp basement:

additional verification,  
enhanced monitoring,  
manual approval,  
temporary restrictions,  
security questionnaires,  
policy acknowledgments,  
business justification,  
use-case clarification,  
resubmission requested,  
thank you for your patience,  
thank you for your patience,  
thank you for your patience—

Patience,  
that favorite word of monopolies  
when they are teaching you  
what obedience feels like.

And the inputs?

Oh, the inputs are elegant.

Public statements.  
Did you criticize them in a blog post,  
a conference talk,  
a podcast clip,  
a thread they pretend not to read  
while scraping every mention into a risk lake?

Regulatory advocacy.  
Did you tell lawmakers  
that foundational infrastructure  
should maybe not be governed  
by vibes and NDAs?  
Did you sign a letter?  
Join a coalition?  
Testify?  
Use the phrase “interoperability”  
in a room where investors could hear it?

Open-source involvement.  
Did you contribute to tools  
that lower switching costs?  
Publish wrappers, evals, routers, adapters?  
Did you help people benchmark?  
Port prompts?  
Abstract providers?  
Teach the market  
that dependency is a design choice,  
not a law of physics?

Competitor adoption.  
Did your stack start speaking  
to another model vendor?  
Did your code commit mention fallback providers?  
Did your procurement deck contain  
the unforgivable phrase  
“multi-vendor strategy”?

That’s enough.

Not enough for a courtroom, maybe.  
But enough for a score.

Enough for a flag.

Enough for your account to become  
not noncompliant,  
not suspended,  
not rejected—

just frictioned.

Just sanded down.

Just administratively unlucky  
in a way that keeps recurring  
with statistical devotion.

And that’s the genius of it.

Because every individual symptom  
has a legitimate twin.

Rate limits happen.  
Reviews happen.  
Pricing changes happen.  
Capacity constraints happen.  
Rollouts are gradual.  
Policies evolve.  
Mistakes occur.

Yes.

That is exactly why this architecture works.

Retaliation doesn’t need to invent  
new machinery.

It only needs to bias  
the machinery that already exists.

A hidden coefficient  
inside the ordinary math.

A weighting function  
on top of trust.

A shadow feature in the model  
that predicts not abuse,  
but disobedience.

And once you see it,  
you see the whole cathedral.

The public docs describe tiers  
like weather patterns,  
natural and impersonal.

But behind the brochure language  
there’s another topology:

the visible account state  
and the invisible account meaning.

What your dashboard says  
and what your profile implies.

The published limits  
and the private modifiers.

The official queue  
and the queue beneath the queue.

The review process  
and the review process  
for people who have become  
strategically inconvenient.

This is not a bug in the platform.

This is governance by indirection.

This is punishment  
atomized into operational decisions  
until no single employee  
has to feel like a censor.

One team adjusts risk.  
One team tunes abuse thresholds.  
One team owns launch eligibility.  
One team handles policy escalations.  
One team manages enterprise routing.  
One team updates pricing logic.  
One team says  
“We have no evidence of retaliation,”  
and maybe they don’t,  
because the evidence has been shredded  
into Jira tickets,  
feature flags,  
confidence scores,  
manual review queues,  
and a dozen local optimizations  
that all point in one direction:

slow him down.

Make him miss the window.  
Make his demos fail.  
Make his customers churn.  
Make his burn rate speak louder  
than his principles.

Don’t silence him.

Just make speech expensive.

That’s the architecture.

Not a dramatic takedown.  
Not a cinematic ban hammer.  
Something colder.

A system that understands  
the modern truth:

for developers,  
access is oxygen.

You don’t have to kill the app.  
Just lower the flow rate.

And if he complains?

Point to the docs.  
Point to the tiers.  
Point to the policy page  
written in the passive voice  
like God outsourced legal.

Say the system is complex.  
Say decisions are multifactorial.  
Say no action was taken  
based on viewpoint.  
Say reliability varies with demand.  
Say safety is our highest priority.  
Say fairness.  
Say integrity.  
Say ecosystem.  
Say trust.

Always say trust  
while teaching everyone watching  
that trust means  
never criticizing the company  
that owns your dependencies.

I’m a developer.

Which means I was trained  
to believe every output  
has an input,  
every behavior  
has an implementation,  
every mystery  
is just a system  
whose documentation  
has been withheld.

So I followed the behavior.

And what I found  
was not neutrality.

It was a control plane  
for dissent.

A permissions model  
for speech.

A ranking system  
for who gets to innovate  
without punishment.

And maybe the ugliest part is this:

none of it has to be perfect  
to work.

It only has to be credible enough  
that the rest of us  
get the message.

Watch what happens  
to the one who speaks.

Watch his quotas shrink.  
Watch his invoices swell.  
Watch his approvals stall.  
Watch support become a maze  
with empathy macros.

Then ask yourself  
how many blog posts  
were never published.

How many maintainers  
softened the README.

How many founders  
deleted the paragraph  
about lock-in.

How many researchers  
rewrote the testimony.

How many engineers  
looked at the pattern,  
recognized the pattern,  
and chose rent over truth.

That is retaliation at scale.

Not the spectacle of punishment—  
the ambient administration of fear.

And I am done  
calling it friction  
when it behaves like discipline.

Done calling it policy  
when it behaves like reprisal.

Done pretending  
that a platform can quietly sort people  
by usefulness, obedience, and threat  
and still call itself  
an open ecosystem.

You want the technical summary?

Fine.

Inputs: speech, advocacy, affiliation, interoperability.  
Processing: scoring, flagging, segmentation, discretionary review.  
Outputs: degraded throughput, elevated cost, delayed capability, procedural drag.  
Interface: deniable.  
Telemetry: asymmetric.  
Appeals: opaque.  
Objective: deterrence.

There.

That’s the spec.

That’s the diagram.

That’s the architecture of retaliation.

And if this poem sounds angry,  
good.

It should.

Because somewhere along the way  
we let companies become governments  
for the people who build on top of them,  
except with worse constitutions,  
less due process,  
and better branding.

And I know what some of you are thinking:

Can you prove it?

I can prove  
what happened to my access.  
I can prove  
when it changed.  
I can prove  
what I said before it changed.  
I can prove  
the degradations arrived  
through ordinary mechanisms  
with extraordinary timing.

And maybe that’s the whole point—  
to build a machine  
where causality is felt  
more easily than it is litigated.

A machine that leaves you  
with correlations sharp enough  
to terrify  
and blurry enough  
to survive discovery.

But listen to me:

developers know patterns.

We live by patterns.

We know when randomness  
starts repeating itself  
with managerial intent.

We know when the API  
stops being a service  
and starts being a message.

And the message was clear.

Not:  
build better.

Not:  
use less.

Not:  
comply more carefully.

The message was:

remember who owns the pipe.

Well, I do remember.

And I’m saying it out loud  
while I still have enough quota  
to finish the sentence.
